newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius finalises policy paper on sugar mills.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius finalises policy paper on sugar mills.

text.p: The government of the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius is finalising its policy paper on centralisation of sugar mills but no date has been given as to when the paper will be published, officials said on Friday.

"It's imperative to rationalise milling activities. We have discussed with all the parties concerned and we have received several suggestions which are viable," Agriculture Minister Arvin Boolell told a news briefing on Friday.
He said the blueprint would set up procedures to be followed if in future there was a need to close down a factory.
"We don't have a programme of which factory to close down and when. But if we receive a demand (to close down a factory) in the future, the blueprint will be called into use."

Mauritius is working on rationalising its sugar mills so as to benefit from economies of scale in production costs and increase sector productivity and competitiveness through modernisation of the factories.

Mauritius Sugar Producers' Association Director Patrick D'Arifat told Reuters in September he expected the consolidation of sugar mills would reduce sugar production units from a present 17 to 13 or 14 by the year 2000.

D'Arifat said the rationalisation process would examine investments in sugar mills, compensation to workers employed by factories which would be asked to close down, and extra transport costs for small cane planters who would have to sell their products to other factories.
Boolell said that by September 1997 he expected 3,700 acres of land to have been converted from tea plantations to sugar.

The land conversion project, expected to span from July 1994 to June 1998, aimed at converting a total of 5,800 acres of land under the public tea sector into sugar cane plantations, increasing sugar output by 18,000 to 20,000 tonnes per year after completion of the programme.
During a normal crop season which is not affected by adverse weather, Mauritius can produce around 650,000 tonnes of sugar per year, industry officials say.
Boolell did not exclude the possibility of seeing more land conversion: "Once private tea growers will see the successful outcome of the programme."
But he did not give any estimate how much extra land could be converted because private growers have still not taken definite decisions towards conversion.
